topic: How does GPS know where you are?
title: Your Phone Has NO Idea Where You Are 🛰️
description: Your phone doesn't know where it is — 30+ satellites and Einstein's relativity do the work.
Signal delay → distance → bubbles that cross at exactly one spot: you.
sources: GPS.gov – Space Segment (constellation, 20,200 km MEO orbit): https://www.gps.gov/systems/gps/space

U.S. Naval Observatory – GPS overview (20,200 km, 12-hour orbits): https://www.cnmoc.usff.navy.mil/our-commands/united-states-naval-observatory/precise-time-department/global-positioning-system/global-positioning-system-overview
Ohio State Univ. (R. Pogge) – Real-world relativity: the GPS navigation system (38 µs/day, ~10 km/day): https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/pogge.1/Ast162/Unit5/gps.html
Penn State GEOG 862 – The navigation solution (4 satellites: x, y, z + clock): https://www.e-education.psu.edu/geog862/node/1724

beats.narration: Your phone has *no idea* where you are.
But over *30 satellites* do, circling 20,200 kilometers above you.
Each one nonstop shouts its *position* and the exact *time*.
That signal needs about *0.07 seconds* to reach you.

data.label: SATELLITE → YOUR PHONE
data.sub: 20,200 km at the speed of light

beats.narration: Your phone measures that delay and turns it into *distance*.
One distance puts you somewhere on a giant *bubble*.
Three bubbles cross at *exactly one spot*: you.
A fourth satellite fixes your phone's cheap clock.
But here's the twist: up there, *time runs faster*.
*38 microseconds* faster every day, thanks to Einstein's relativity.
Ignore it, and your map drifts about *10 kilometers* a day.
